lesson.title: Servers: The End Systems That Wait to Be Asked
lesson.summary: Defines the server as an end system whose role is to provide a service on request, always available and addressable, and explains what makes serving different from ordinary end system behavior.
lesson.body:
Not all end systems behave the same way in a conversation. Some sit and wait, ready to respond the instant someone asks for something. These are servers: end systems dedicated to providing a specific service, such as delivering a webpage, storing an email, answering a domain name lookup, or streaming a video, to other end systems that ask for it. A server does not usually initiate contact. Instead, it listens continuously, and when a request arrives, it processes that request and sends back a response.

This waiting posture shapes how servers are built and operated in practice. Because a server needs to be reachable at any moment, it is typically kept running continuously and is assigned a stable, well-known address so that other end systems can find it reliably. A home laptop that only checks email once a day and then goes to sleep would make a poor server, since nobody could count on reaching it. A machine in a data center that never powers down and always answers on the same address is a much better fit, which is why most servers today live in data centers or cloud platforms built for exactly that kind of always-on reliability.

The word "server" also describes a role rather than a fixed category of hardware. Technically, any end system can run server software and start behaving like a server, a personal computer running a small web server program is, for as long as that program runs, genuinely serving requests. In practice, though, the demands of serving many requests reliably and continuously mean that dedicated, purpose built machines usually take on the job, while ordinary end systems like laptops and phones rarely do.

A single popular server rarely handles its workload alone. A busy website might receive far more requests each second than one machine can comfortably answer, so real world services typically run many servers behind the scenes, spreading incoming requests across them so no single machine becomes overwhelmed. From the outside, this collection of machines is usually presented to the world as though it were one server with one address, even though many physical or virtual machines may be cooperating to answer requests. This is one reason large organizations invest in data centers full of servers rather than relying on a single powerful computer.

Consider a concrete example: when a company hosts its website, it runs web server software on a machine that stays powered on and connected around the clock. That machine is assigned a stable network address, and it listens for incoming requests. When someone types the company's website address into a browser, a request travels across the network to that server, the server retrieves the requested page and sends it back. If the server were turned off, the website would become unreachable, which is why organizations invest heavily in keeping their servers available.

Servers are one half of the most common pattern for organizing communication on the internet: the client server model. This section has defined the server side of that pattern, the end system that waits and responds. The next section introduces its counterpart, the client, the end system that reaches out and asks.
